subject: arvr
title: Unit 4 MCQs — IO Modalities, AI and Behaviour

items.q: In the realm of tracking methods for AR, what distinguishes **sparse** tracking from **dense** tracking?
options: Sparse tracking primarily captures individual points, while dense tracking involves continuous tracking of body parts
Sparse tracking restricts interaction to a few points, while dense tracking relies on a detailed understanding of the environment
Sparse tracking is suitable for arbitrary changes in the environment, while dense tracking focuses on capturing specific body parts
Sparse tracking deals with discrete points, whereas dense tracking utilizes rich sensory input for continuous tracking of body parts
items.explain: **Sparse** operates on **discrete interest points** and deliberately discards most of the image, which is what makes it fast. **Dense** uses **rich sensory input** — typically a depth sensor — to track every pixel, enabling continuous body-part tracking, reconstruction and **occlusion handling**.

items.q: Why is computer vision essential to AR, given that headsets already have IMUs?
options: IMUs cannot measure rotation
IMUs cannot supply position — a bias double-integrates into quadratic error, so an absolute spatial reference is needed
Cameras are cheaper than IMUs
IMUs only work outdoors
items.explain: Unit 3 ended at exactly this wall. Inertial sensing gives orientation but **never position**; outside a prepared room the only sensor that supplies an absolute spatial reference is the **camera**. Vision closes the loop inertial sensing cannot.

items.q: Why do the four corners of a square marker yield a full 6DOF pose from a single image?
options: Because four points is the minimum for any pose estimate
Because the marker's 3D geometry is known, giving four 3D↔2D correspondences — a Perspective-n-Point problem
Because the camera must be perpendicular to the marker
Because the marker encodes its pose in its pattern
items.explain: **Known geometry converts a single image into an absolute pose.** The marker is a square of known size, so you know the corners' 3D coordinates; observing their 2D projections gives a small **PnP** problem. The interior pattern supplies **identity** and resolves the 90° rotational ambiguity.

items.q: Which advantage of marker tracking is **impossible** for a single camera tracking natural features?
options: Working in low light
Recovering absolute metric scale
Running in real time
Detecting corners
items.explain: A monocular camera cannot distinguish a doll's house from a real house — identical images. Because you **told the system the marker is 8 cm across**, marker tracking gets absolute scale for free. This is why markers are still used to **bootstrap SLAM maps with correct scale**.

items.q: In the stereo camera tracking pipeline for rigid-body marker-based motion tracking, what is the purpose of the step involving **epipolar geometry**?
options: To determine the target's pose using absolute orientation
To perform blob detection in all images to locate the spheres of the rigid body markers
To establish point correspondences between blobs
To match 3D candidate points to 3D target points
items.explain: Camera A sees five bright dots and camera B sees five — **which is which?** The epipolar constraint says a point seen at $\mathbf x_A$ must lie on a **single line** in camera B, turning a 2D search into a **1D** one. The other options are stages ①, ④ and ⑤ of the pipeline.

items.q: Why do retro-reflective spheres appear as bright dots on a black background in an IR tracking system?
options: They emit their own infrared light
Retro-reflective material returns light straight back toward its source, and the cameras are ringed with IR LEDs
The cameras use long exposures
The spheres are heated and detected thermally
items.explain: Each camera has an **IR LED ring**; retro-reflective material returns light **back toward its source**, so from the camera's viewpoint the spheres blaze while everything else stays dark. The image becomes trivially easy to process — **engineering the image rather than the algorithm**.

items.q: The final stage of the multi-camera IR pipeline uses **absolute orientation**. What kind of problem is it?
options: A 3D↔2D correspondence problem, solved iteratively
A 3D↔3D alignment problem with a closed-form solution
A 2D↔2D homography estimation
A non-linear optimisation requiring an initial guess
items.explain: Because triangulation has already produced 3D points, aligning them to the body's known 3D points is **3D↔3D** — solvable in **closed form** (Horn's method / SVD), with no iteration or initial guess. Contrast marker tracking, which is **3D↔2D** (PnP) because it has only one camera.

items.q: Why are **corners** preferred over edges or flat regions as interest points?
options: Corners are brighter than other regions
A flat region gives no information and an edge is ambiguous along its length; only a corner is localisable in both directions
Corners are rarer, so there are fewer to process
Edges cannot be detected in colour images
items.explain: Shift a window over a flat region — nothing changes. Shift along an edge — nothing changes (**the aperture problem**). Shift at a corner — it changes in **every** direction. Two dimensions of information means fully localisable.

items.q: What makes **FAST** fast?
options: It uses a GPU
It tests only four compass pixels first and rejects most candidates after four comparisons
It processes every fourth pixel
It uses a smaller image resolution
items.explain: For a contiguous arc of 9 out of 16 circle pixels to exist, at least **three of the four compass points** must be consistently brighter or darker. Most pixels fail this and are discarded immediately — which is what makes FAST usable at video rate on a phone.

items.q: What does a **descriptor** provide that a **detector** does not?
options: The location of the feature
A representation of the local appearance, allowing the same point to be matched across images
The rotation of the camera
The depth of the feature
items.explain: **Detector finds; descriptor recognises.** Knowing there is a corner at pixel (312, 88) says nothing about **which** corner it is. The descriptor turns a set of points into a set of **identities**, enabling matching across frames or against a map.

items.q: In the tracking-by-detection pipeline for sparse interest points, what is the order of the five stages?
options: Descriptor Creation → PnP camera pose determination → Interest Point Detection → Descriptor Matching → Robust Pose Estimation
Interest Point Detection → Descriptor Creation → Descriptor Matching → Perspective-n-Point camera pose determination → Robust Pose Estimation
Robust Pose Estimation → Descriptor Matching → Interest Point Detection → PnP camera pose determination → Descriptor Creation
PnP camera pose determination → Descriptor Creation → Interest Point Detection → Descriptor Matching → Robust Pose Estimation
items.explain: **Detect → describe → match → PnP → robust estimation.** The distractors permute these — most commonly putting pose determination **before** matching, which is impossible: you need **correspondences** before you can solve for pose.

items.q: Why is **RANSAC** required in the final stage of tracking by detection?
options: To speed up descriptor matching
Because descriptor matching always produces outliers, and least-squares fitting is not robust to them
To detect more interest points
To compute the camera's intrinsic parameters
items.explain: Repeated textures, similar corners and moving objects guarantee wrong matches. RANSAC **guesses a minimal sample, assumes it is clean, and counts how many others agree** — consensus identifies the good data, and only then do you fit.

items.q: What is the key advantage of tracking **by detection** over incremental tracking?
options: It is computationally cheaper
It is stateless — no drift accumulates and it recovers from tracking loss instantly
It needs no pre-built map
It produces smoother pose estimates
items.explain: Each frame is solved **from scratch**, so nothing accumulates and nothing needs recovering. The costs are the opposite of the benefits: it is **expensive every frame** and **requires a pre-built map** of descriptors with 3D positions.

items.q: In the classic approach to incremental tracking, what is the primary technique employed by the **Kanade-Lucas-Tomasi (KLT)** tracker?
options: KLT uses histogram analysis for feature extraction and rigid body transformations to model image changes
KLT utilizes blob detection for tracking and non-linear transformations to model image changes
KLT combines template matching for tracking
KLT employs feature extraction followed by optical flow tracking
items.explain: **Feature extraction followed by optical flow tracking.** KLT finds corners then solves the optical-flow constraint over a small window — which is solvable precisely where the structure tensor has **two large eigenvalues**, i.e. at a corner. Hence *'Good Features to Track'*.

items.q: Which camera motion model is the **common default** for active search during incremental tracking?
options: Constant position
Constant velocity
Constant acceleration
Random walk
items.explain: **Constant velocity** suits smooth panning and walking. **IMU-driven** prediction is better still when available — the gyroscope reports actual motion at 1000 Hz, telling the vision system exactly where to look. A tighter prediction means a smaller search window: faster, and less likely to latch onto the wrong feature.

items.q: Which is the principal **drawback** of incremental tracking?
options: It requires a pre-built map
Drift accumulates without bound, and it cannot recover once lost
It cannot run in real time
It only works with markers
items.explain: Small per-frame errors compound — the **same phenomenon as gyroscope drift**, and for the same reason: you are integrating **relative** measurements. The cure is identical too: correct periodically against something **absolute** — tracking by detection, or loop closure.

items.q: In the **PTAM** system, how do the responsibilities of the Tracking Thread and Mapping Thread differ?
options: The Tracking Thread operates at a slow rate adding keyframes, while the Mapping Thread works at full frame rate computing camera poses
The Tracking Thread runs slowly adding keyframes, while the Mapping Thread operates at full frame rate
The Tracking Thread operates at full frame rate computing camera poses from correspondences, while the Mapping Thread runs at a much slower rate focusing on adding new keyframes
Both threads operate at the same frame rate, computing camera poses and searching for correspondences
items.explain: **Tracking feeds the display, so it must never be late; mapping improves the map, so it can afford to think.** The distractors swap the two. Before PTAM both ran in one loop, so every frame paid the cost of map optimisation.

items.q: What problem does **loop closure** solve in SLAM?
options: It detects when the camera has stopped moving
It recognises a previously-visited place and corrects accumulated drift
It closes the mapping thread when the map is complete
It removes dynamic objects from the map
items.explain: Loop closure is the **visual equivalent of an absolute reference**. Incremental tracking drifts as a gyroscope does; recognising a mapped place is a measurement that **does not depend on history**, so it can cancel accumulated error — producing SLAM's characteristic map 'snap'.

items.q: What does **model-free** mean in the definition of SLAM?
options: It does not use a camera model
It requires no prior knowledge of the environment
It does not build a map
It uses no machine learning models
items.explain: Unlike marker-based or model-based tracking, SLAM needs **no prior model of the environment** — walk into an unfamiliar room and it starts working. That is why it powers every modern inside-out headset and phone AR platform.

items.q: Why does the **essential matrix** have only 5 degrees of freedom?
options: Because it is a 3×3 matrix with 4 fixed entries
3 for rotation + 3 for translation, minus 1 because translation magnitude is unrecoverable from images
Because it only applies to calibrated stereo pairs
Because RANSAC discards 4 degrees of freedom
items.explain: Hence the **5-point algorithm**. The missing degree of freedom is **absolute scale** — a large scene far away and a small scene close up produce identical images (the doll's-house problem).

items.q: How does the use of epipolar geometry in **visual odometry** differ from its use in **multi-camera IR tracking**?
options: They use different equations
In IR tracking the relative pose is known and correspondences are sought; in VO the correspondences are known and the relative pose is sought
VO does not use epipolar geometry
IR tracking uses the essential matrix; VO uses the fundamental matrix
items.explain: **Same equation, opposite unknown.** In IR tracking, calibration gives the cameras' relative pose, so epipolar geometry **finds correspondences**. In VO, feature tracking gives correspondences, so epipolar geometry **finds the pose**.

items.q: What distinguishes **visual odometry** from full **SLAM**?
options: VO uses two cameras; SLAM uses one
VO estimates the trajectory only, with no persistent map or loop closure, so its drift is unbounded
VO works indoors; SLAM works outdoors
VO requires markers
items.explain: **VO is the front end of SLAM without the memory.** It answers *'how did I move?'* frame by frame and drifts without bound. SLAM adds a persistent map and **loop closure**, converting unbounded drift into bounded error.

items.q: In outdoor AR, what is the division of labour between GPS and vision?
options: GPS handles orientation; vision handles position
GPS says which building you are near; vision says exactly where on it to draw
GPS is used indoors; vision is used outdoors
They are alternatives — only one is used at a time
items.explain: GPS is **1–100 m** accurate — far too coarse for registration, but it **bounds the error globally** so vision needn't search a whole city. Vision then refines to centimetre alignment. Neither could do the job alone.

items.q: How does a **bag-of-words** model enable large-scale place recognition?
options: It stores every image in a database and compares them pixel by pixel
It quantises descriptors into visual words and represents each image as a histogram, searchable via an inverted index
It uses GPS coordinates as keys
It compresses images using JPEG
items.explain: **Throw away the geometry, then put it back.** Discarding *where* features are and keeping only *which* are present makes an image a sparse vector searchable in milliseconds — then **geometric verification** with RANSAC confirms the shortlist. Cheap-and-approximate to shortlist; expensive-and-exact to confirm.

items.q: What does **GIS data integration** contribute to outdoor tracking?
options: Faster GPS fixes
Building outlines and elevation models — a prior geometry that constrains pose search and enables occlusion
Higher camera resolution
Wireless connectivity
items.explain: **Constraints are information** — the same principle as the skeleton prior in Unit 3. Knowing a building's footprint and height turns an open-ended pose search into fitting the observed skyline to a known model, and supplies the geometry needed to **occlude** virtual content correctly.

items.q: Why does AR need 3D scanning in addition to tracking?
options: To improve GPS accuracy
Because occlusion, physics, surface placement and realistic lighting all require scene geometry, not just camera pose
To reduce the polygon count
To calibrate the IMU
items.explain: Tracking answers *'where is the camera?'*; scanning answers *'what shape is the scene?'*. Without it you get a **floating** object — correctly positioned but passing through furniture and casting no shadow. It is the difference between an overlay and an augmentation.

items.q: Which 3D scanning method fails on **textureless** surfaces such as a plain white wall?
options: Structured light
Time-of-Flight
Stereo vision
LIDAR
items.explain: **Stereo** is passive — it matches pixels between two views, and a blank wall offers nothing to match. **Active** methods (structured light, ToF, LIDAR) supply their own light and work fine. The two questions when choosing: *is there texture?* and *is there sunlight?*

items.q: In the reconstruction pipeline, what is the purpose of fusing depth data into a **TSDF** volume rather than keeping a raw point cloud?
options: To compress the data
Averaging many noisy observations cancels noise and defines a true surface, which a point cloud cannot
To convert to colour
To speed up capture
items.explain: A raw point cloud is noisy and has **no notion of surface** — you cannot tell inside from outside, so you cannot render occlusion or run physics. A **Truncated Signed Distance Field** stores signed distance per voxel; the surface is where it crosses zero. **KinectFusion** was the landmark demonstration.

items.q: What is **gorilla arm**?
options: A tracking failure when the arm occludes the sensor
Fatigue from holding the arm unsupported in mid-air to interact
A gesture used to summon a menu
Distortion of the arm in the avatar's inverse kinematics
items.explain: The deltoid is not built for sustained static load — mid-air interfaces feel magical for thirty seconds and exhausting after two minutes. Mitigations: keep interaction **below shoulder height**, prefer **short gestures**, allow the arm to rest, and use **gaze or voice** for frequent actions.

items.q: A virtual toolbelt that stays at the user's waist as they walk and turn is an example of:
options: Head-referenced placement
Torso-referenced placement
Hand-referenced placement
World-referenced placement
items.explain: **Torso-referenced** — content fixed relative to the body. It is **out of the way** (unlike head-referenced, which always occludes the view) and therefore requires a deliberate look or turn to access. That is the availability-versus-intrusiveness trade.

items.q: Which display technology fundamentally limits **physical–virtual coherence** because it cannot occlude the real world?
options: Video see-through
Optical see-through
Spatial projection
Handheld magic lens
items.explain: An optical combiner **adds** light and cannot subtract it, so a virtual object can never hide what is behind it. This is a large part of why **video see-through** has gained commercial ground despite adding latency.

items.q: Why is **gaze** rarely used as a standalone selection modality?
options: It is too slow
The Midas touch problem — you cannot look at something without selecting it
Eye trackers are too expensive
It cannot be tracked in a headset
items.explain: Gaze is the **fastest** pointing modality — the eye reaches a target before the hand starts moving. But you cannot look without selecting, so the standard fix is **gaze-and-commit**: gaze to point, a separate channel (pinch, dwell, voice) to confirm.

items.q: **LucidTouch** is the named example of which input modality?
options: Gestures
Touch — specifically back-of-device interaction
Voice commands
Body tracking
items.explain: A **see-through** mobile device sensing touch on its **back**, so the fingers don't obscure the screen. It addresses the **fat finger problem**: on a small display the finger hides the very target it is selecting.

items.q: Why do VR controllers persist despite hand tracking being available?
options: Hand tracking does not work in VR
Controllers give buttons (no Midas touch), haptic feedback, proprioceptive grip and arm support
Controllers are cheaper than cameras
Hand tracking cannot achieve 6DOF
items.explain: Controllers solve exactly what free-hand gestures cannot: **unambiguous discrete input**, **felt confirmation**, a physical object your proprioception can locate without looking, and a natural lower hand position that **reduces gorilla arm**.

items.q: In multimodal interaction, what is each modality typically best suited to?
options: Speech for pointing; gesture for naming
Speech for verbs and names; gaze and gesture for deixis (this, that, there)
Both are equivalent and interchangeable
Gesture for confirmation; speech for precision
items.explain: The canonical demonstration is **'Put that there'** (Bolt, 1980). Speech cannot say *which* object without a name; pointing cannot express the *action*. Combining them lets you drop the awkward parts of each — and adds robustness, since the channels cover each other's failures.

items.q: What is a **magic lens** in AR?
options: A physical lens that magnifies the display
A movable window that reveals augmented information about whatever is behind it
A projector that maps content onto surfaces
A filter that removes real-world clutter
items.explain: **Augmented browsing overlays** used for navigation and tourism. Rather than augmenting everything (unreadable clutter), you augment **only what is inside the lens**. Every handheld phone AR app is a magic lens — you move the window, not the world.

items.q: The **Phantom Omni** is an example of which kind of haptic device?
options: Tactile — stimulating skin receptors with vibration
Kinaesthetic — applying forces felt by muscles and joints
Mid-air ultrasonic haptics
Thermal feedback
items.explain: An articulated stylus arm that both **tracks** 6DOF pose and **applies forces** back through the linkage — push into a virtual surface and it pushes back. Its tracking is **mechanical**, which is unavoidable: force feedback needs something to brace against.

items.q: Why must haptic force feedback update at around **1000 Hz**?
options: To match the IMU sample rate
Because touch is far more temporally acute than vision — below that, hard surfaces feel spongy or buzz
Because the GPU renders at that rate
To avoid aliasing in the force signal
items.explain: The haptic counterpart of the visual **20 ms** budget. You can feel a discontinuity of a millisecond as a buzz, whereas vision integrates over tens of milliseconds. **A surface updating at 60 Hz does not feel solid — it feels like jelly.**

items.q: Why is spatial audio disproportionately valuable in AR/VR?
options: It is cheaper to render than graphics
Hearing is omnidirectional while the visual field of view is narrow, so sound can direct attention outside the display
It reduces motion sickness
It replaces the need for haptics
items.explain: A visual cue outside the (narrow) headset field of view is simply invisible; a **sound behind you** is heard immediately and tells you where to look. It is the natural channel for **notification and guidance**.

items.q: What is the primary mechanism through which sound is produced, and how is the perceptual experience created in human ears?
options: Sound is generated by electromagnetic waves; perception results from variations in electrical charge
Sound is produced by the displacement of molecules in a medium causing pressure variations; perception arises from displacement of the eardrum, converted into sound pressure levels in decibels
Sound is generated through movement of particles in a vacuum; perception is facilitated by variations in particle density
Sound is created by the emission of light waves; perception is achieved through absorption of these light waves
items.explain: Sound is a **longitudinal pressure wave** requiring a **medium** — it cannot travel through a vacuum, because it *is* the motion of the medium. The distractors invoke electromagnetic waves, vacuums and light.

items.q: The audible frequency range and the speed of sound at 20 °C are:
options: 20 Hz – 20 kHz, and 343.2 m/s
20 Hz – 2 kHz, and 343.2 km/s
2 Hz – 20 kHz, and 1500 m/s
200 Hz – 20 kHz, and 331 m/s
items.explain: **Infrasound < 20 Hz · audible 20 Hz – 20 kHz · ultrasound > 20 kHz**, and **343.2 m/s at 20 °C**. That speed is why ultrasonic tracking is slow (a 3 m round trip costs ~9 ms) and why **ITD** works (~640 µs maximum delay between the ears).

items.q: Why does audio occlusion behave as a **filter** rather than a binary block, unlike visual occlusion?
options: Because sound travels slower than light
Because diffraction is frequency-dependent — low frequencies bend around obstacles while high frequencies are blocked
Because sound reflects more than light
Because the ear is less sensitive than the eye
items.explain: Audible wavelengths (**1.7 cm to 17 m**) are comparable to doors, furniture and people, so waves diffract strongly around objects of similar size. Light's ~500 nm wavelength never diffracts at human scale. Hence a voice around a corner is **muffled**, not silent.

items.q: Which binaural cue dominates at **low** frequencies, and why?
options: ILD, because the head shadows low frequencies most
ITD, because above ~1.5 kHz the wavelength is shorter than the ear spacing and phase becomes ambiguous
ITD, because low frequencies travel faster
Neither — low frequencies cannot be localised
items.explain: **Duplex theory.** **ITD** compares phase, which wraps ambiguously once the wavelength (~22 cm at 1.5 kHz) drops below the ear spacing. **ILD** needs the head to cast an acoustic shadow, which requires the wavelength to be smaller than the head — long waves simply **diffract around it**.

items.q: What is the **cone of confusion**, and how is it resolved?
options: The region where two speakers interfere; resolved by moving them apart
A surface of positions giving identical binaural cues; resolved by head movements and pinna filtering
The frequency band where ITD and ILD overlap; resolved by equalisation
The area behind the listener where sound cannot be heard
items.explain: A sound directly in front and directly behind give the **same ITD and ILD**. **Head movements** change the cues differently for front and back, resolving it instantly — which is a strong argument for **head-tracked spatial audio** in VR.

items.q: The **precedence effect** states that:
options: Louder sounds are perceived first
The early-arriving sound dominates perception of direction despite later echoes
High frequencies are perceived before low frequencies
The last sound heard determines the perceived location
items.explain: Also the Haas effect or **law of the first wavefront**. It is why you can localise a speaker in a reverberant room at all. For VR audio it means the **direct path must be accurate and low-latency, while reflections can be approximated** — they contribute spaciousness, not direction.

items.q: **Stevens' power law** for loudness implies that:
options: Perceived loudness is proportional to intensity
Doubling perceived loudness requires roughly ten times the acoustic power
Loudness is independent of frequency
The ear responds linearly above 1 kHz
items.explain: $\psi = k\phi^{a}$ with $a \approx 0.67$ for loudness. This is why sound is measured in **decibels** and why **volume controls are logarithmic** — a linear slider driving linear gain feels wrong, since half the travel produces nearly all the perceived change.

items.q: Which reactive AI technique scores every possible action against the current world state and picks the highest?
options: Finite state machine
Behaviour tree
Utility AI
Goal-oriented action planning
items.explain: **Utility AI** — $U(a) = \sum w_i f_i(\text{state})$. It is the **most adaptable** of the three because behaviour degrades gracefully as the situation changes, at the cost of being **harder to predict and debug**. GOAP is deliberative, not reactive.

items.q: Why did behaviour trees largely replace finite state machines for NPC behaviour?
options: They run faster
Priority is implicit in the tree structure, so adding a behaviour means inserting one subtree rather than re-wiring n transitions
They can plan ahead
They require no authoring
items.explain: FSM transitions grow as $O(n^2)$ — **combinatorial explosion**. Behaviour trees give **modularity**: reusable subtrees, and automatic interruption when a higher-priority branch's condition becomes true, with no explicit transition needed.

items.q: On which of the four properties does reactive AI score **best**?
options: Adaptability
Universality
Feasibility
Complexity handling
items.explain: **Feasibility** — trivial runtime cost, **predictable and debuggable**, authorable by designers without programming, and guaranteed to meet frame budgets. It scores poorly on adaptability (bounded by what was authored), universality (doesn't transfer) and complexity (authoring burden grows steeply).

items.q: Which problem class is **best suited** to deliberative rather than reactive AI?
options: Playing an idle animation
Resource management, where the best action now depends on future consumption
Turning to face the player
Playing a footstep sound
items.explain: The three classes named are **resource management, tactical planning and intelligent exploration** — all share the feature that **the best action now depends on what happens later**, which a reactive rule (a function of the present only) cannot express.

items.q: What are the two stated trade-offs of deliberative AI?
options: Less accurate and less adaptable
Less controllable than reactive AI, and computationally intensive (though it can be offloaded offline)
Slower to author and harder to animate
Requires more memory and more sensors
items.explain: 'Less controllable' is a genuine problem — a planner may find a technically optimal solution that ruins a designed set-piece. 'Offloaded offline' is the mitigation: plan ahead, plan on a **background thread**, or plan coarsely while a reactive layer handles the moment-to-moment.

items.q: In a hybrid AI architecture, how are the layers arranged?
options: Reactive on top setting goals for a deliberative layer below
Deliberative on top setting sub-goals for a fast reactive layer below
Both run at the same rate and vote
They alternate frame by frame
items.explain: **Fast-and-dumb underneath, slow-and-smart on top** — the same layered, multi-timescale architecture as IMU under vision, incremental tracking under relocalisation, and PTAM's tracking thread under its mapping thread.

items.q: What is the primary mechanism for guiding an agent to learn behaviours in a dynamic and interactive environment?
options: The agent learns through pre-programmed instructions, ensuring a static learning process
Learning relies on supervised techniques, allowing the agent to learn autonomously without guidance
The agent is guided through a punishment function, emphasising consequences for incorrect actions
The agent is guided to the desired behaviour through a reward function, promoting positive outcomes for correct actions
items.explain: **Reinforcement learning** guides behaviour through a **reward function**. Pre-programmed instructions aren't learning; RL is not supervised (there are no labelled correct actions); and while rewards can be negative, the mechanism is framed as a **reward** function.

items.q: An autonomous vehicle is trained to mimic a human expert's driving. Which statement about **imitation learning** is accurate?
options: It learns from pre-recorded scenarios without any human demonstration
The vehicle observes and mimics the expert's actions, using a dataset of expert demonstrations to acquire a decision-making policy
It relies exclusively on reinforcement signals from the environment, with no reference to human demonstrations
Its goal is to let the human expert directly control the vehicle during training
items.explain: Imitation learning acquires a **policy from expert demonstrations** — no reward function required. Option (c) describes plain RL; (a) contradicts the definition; (d) describes teleoperation, not learning.

items.q: What is the principal weakness of **behaviour cloning**?
options: It requires a hand-designed reward function
Compounding error — trained only on states the expert visited, a small mistake leads to unfamiliar states and the error snowballs
It cannot be trained on video data
It is slower than inverse RL
items.explain: The classic illustration: a policy cloned from perfect driving has **never seen the car drifting toward the kerb**, so it never learned to recover. **IRL and GAIL** are more robust because they recover the **intent** rather than copying actions.

items.q: How does **Inverse Reinforcement Learning** differ from behaviour cloning?
options: It uses a larger neural network
It infers the reward function the expert was optimising, rather than copying the action mapping
It requires no demonstrations
It only works for discrete action spaces
items.explain: Behaviour cloning learns *'here, they turned left'*; IRL learns *'they were trying to stay in the lane'*. Because it recovers the **goal**, an IRL agent can act sensibly in situations the expert never demonstrated — including recovering from mistakes.

items.q: Which pair of models is named for **object recognition** in AR scene labelling?
options: ResNet and VGG
YOLO and SSD
GAN and VAE
KLT and Harris
items.explain: **YOLO and SSD** are **single-pass** detectors — one forward pass produces all boxes and classes at once. Earlier detectors ran a classifier over many candidate regions, which was far too slow for a frame budget.

items.q: Which technique is named for **procedural content generation** in VR environment synthesis?
options: Reinforcement learning
GANs
Optical flow
Bag-of-words
items.explain: **GANs** for generating textures, terrain and layouts. The five named applications are: object recognition (**YOLO/SSD**), gesture recognition (**optical flow, KLT**), **SLAM with neural nets**, procedural content generation (**GANs**) and adaptive NPCs (**RL**).
